summary: Defines a standard SNMP MIB for ADSL lines, based on the ADSL Forum data model, so providers can manage them.

eli5.summary: A control panel with readouts for broadband phone-line connections, so a company can see how each line is doing.

subtitle: A standard SNMP MIB that lets managers monitor and configure ADSL lines at both the ATU-C and ATU-R ends.

tldr.problem: Providers that run many ADSL lines need a common way to read line status and performance and to set configuration, regardless of vendor.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an SMIv2 MIB based on the ADSL Forum data model. Each ADSL line appears as interfaces in the IF-MIB (a physical one plus fast and/or interleaved channels), with tables for status, performance counters in 15-minute and 1-day buckets, shared configuration profiles, and traps for threshold crossings.
tldr.outcome: A line is managed through one set of objects for both ends of the link, with the ATU-R agent supporting only a subset.

today: RFC 2662 is a Proposed Standard published in August 1999, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Scope and the SNMP Framework
sections.content:
RFC 2662 defines a standard SNMP MIB (Management Information Base) for ADSL lines, based on the ADSL Forum standard data model. The ADSL standard describes the ATU-C and ATU-R as the two sides of the ADSL line, and this MIB covers the view from both agents. Each instance in the MIB represents a single ADSL line. The ADSL Forum Network Management Working Group provided input.

The module is written in SMIv2. The RFC lists the five parts of the SNMP management framework (architecture, structure of management information, message protocols, protocol operations and applications) and notes that an SMIv1 version can be produced by translation, except for things such as Counter64 that have no translation. Objects are named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER and accessed through the MIB as a virtual information store.
sections.eli5: A MIB is a big list of questions you are allowed to ask a device, such as how fast is this line. This one covers phone-line internet connections.

sections.title: ADSL Lines in the Interface Tables
sections.content:
The MIB integrates with the IF-MIB (RFC 2233). IANA assigned three ifTypes: adsl(94) for the physical interface, adslInterleave(124) for the interleaved channel and adslFast(125) for the fast channel. A physical interface always exists for each ADSL line; the fast and interleaved channel interfaces exist depending on the operational configuration.

Generic interface attributes such as ifIndex, ifSpeed and ifOperStatus are not duplicated in the ADSL MIB. For example, ifSpeed is the transmit rate from the agent's perspective (line rate for the physical interface, channel rate for channels), and ifPhysAddress should be a zero-length octet string. The ifStackTable links each channel entry to its physical entry, which matters because configuration is kept only with the physical-layer entry. The ifRcvAddressTable is not applicable.

Implementing the Entity MIB (RFC 2037) is optional and does not change the information required here. It can present DSLAM components such as shelves, line cards and ports and map them to interfaces.
sections.eli5: Each phone line gets one main entry, and its fast and slow lanes get their own smaller entries linked back to it, like rooms listed under one house address.

sections.title: Naming Conventions and Table Structure
sections.content:
The MIB uses several parallel tables: line (common attributes), ATU-C and ATU-R status, performance tables and profile tables. Separate tables cover the physical layer and the channel layer, and one set of channel tables serves both fast and interleaved channels, told apart by ifType. There are two identical sets of data for ATU-C and ATU-R because that is easier to read than shared tables. Line Code Specific MIBs are intended to sit under adslLCSMib.

The terms transmit and receive are from the perspective of the table's own end of the line, so adslAtucChanConfFastMaxTxRate is the downstream rate and adslAturChanConfFastMaxTxRate is the upstream rate. Abbreviations include Lof, Lol, Los and Lpr (loss of framing, link, signal and power), ES (errored second), Atn, Psd and Snr (attenuation, power spectral density, signal to noise ratio). A Loss of Link is declared at the ATU-C when a Loss of Signal is not preceded by a dying-gasp message from the ATU-R, and is only supported by the ATU-C.

The adslLineType object tells which of five operational configurations the line has: no channels, fast only, interleaved only, fast or interleaved (the manager picks one) and fast and interleaved. The physical entry exists in all of them.
sections.eli5: There are matching sets of readouts for each end of the line, and a line can have a fast lane, a slow safer lane, both, or neither.

sections.title: Configuration Profiles
sections.content:
A managed node may handle hundreds or thousands of ADSL lines, so setting every parameter on every line would be burdensome. The MIB therefore defines two profile tables, one for configuration and one for alarms, and a way to attach lines to profiles. Profile tables can be implemented in one of two modes, but not both at once.

MODE-I, dynamic profiles: the manager creates and deletes profiles, each named by an administratively assigned SnmpAdminString. Several lines can share one profile (for example one called silver), and a change to the profile reconfigures all lines that use it. A profile must be unreferenced from all lines before it is deleted. Implementations MUST provide a default profile named DEFVAL for each profile type, with vendor-specific values unless the RFC says otherwise.

MODE-II, static profiles: the agent automatically creates one profile per physical line, named by the line's index, and managers cannot create or delete profiles. The related objects are read-only.
sections.eli5: Instead of setting the rules for each line by hand, you make a few plans like silver and gold and point many lines at the plan they should follow.

sections.title: Counters, Intervals and Traps
sections.content:
For physical-level events (ES, Los, Lof, Lol, Lpr and line initialization attempts) there are event counters, a current 15-minute bucket, up to 96 history buckets of 15 minutes each, and current and previous 1-day counters. Channel-level counters cover received blocks, received-and-corrected blocks, received-but-uncorrectable blocks and transmitted blocks. Counters are not reset when an ATU-C or ATU-R is reinitialized, only when the agent is reset or reinitialized. Agents need not align 15-minute intervals to the wall clock.

Required traps are coldStart and warmStart (per agent) and linkUp and linkDown (per interface). A linkDown is generated for Lof, Los, Lol, loss of signal quality or Lpr events, and the status objects give detail. The MIB adds traps for initialization failure, rate change and threshold crossings of Lofs, Lols, Loss, Lprs and ESs. Each threshold has its own value, and 0 disables the trap.

A threshold trap fires when the current 15-minute counter becomes equal to or exceeds the threshold, once per interval per interface. Setting a threshold to 1 gives a trap whenever the event occurs, at most once per 15 minutes. The rate change trap fires when a channel's transmit rate rises by the Up threshold or falls by the Down threshold relative to the previous value, which is updated at initialization and whenever a trap is sent, so small changes accumulate.
sections.eli5: The line keeps score of problems in 15-minute chunks and a daily total. If the problems pass a limit you chose, it rings a bell, but only once per chunk.

sections.title: ATU-C and ATU-R Conformance Groups
sections.content:
Objects fall into two conformance groups. All objects in the MIB module are supported by an ATU-C agent, while an ATU-R agent supports only a portion. Figure 7 of the RFC lists them. For example, the ATU-R agent does not support the adslLineConfProfileTable, does not support the Lol and Lpr counters in the ATU-C performance table, and supports all of the ATU-R tables.

The ATU-R agent supports the rate change, Lofs, Loss and ESs traps for both ends, plus the ATU-R Lprs trap. The reason is that the SNMP agent likely lives with only one end of the line, so the far end status can be incomplete: when the line has errors, the far-end unit may not be able to report them correctly.
sections.eli5: The box at the phone company can answer every question, but the box in the customer's home can only answer some of them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC raises three points. First, blocking unauthorized access to the MIB is outside its scope, but access would let an intruder change profiles, which could disturb subscriber service (for example rate settings) and network operations (for example trap thresholds such as SNR margins).

Second, some objects, notably those that reveal which vendor's equipment is in use, may be sensitive, so read access may need controlling. SNMPv1 is called an insecure environment on its own, and the RFC recommends considering SNMPv3, specifically the User-based Security Model (RFC 2574) and the View-based Access Control Model (RFC 2575).

Third, ADSL connectivity from the ATU-R lets a subscriber manipulate their own link, and unfiltered fluctuations could generate enough traps to overwhelm the management interface or element manager.
sections.eli5: Whoever can change the settings could mess up other people's service, so only the right people should get the keys, and a customer should not be able to flood the system with alarms.
